concepts.name: Constitutional Basis and Scope of Article 123
key_dimensions: Exact text and structure of Article 123 — conditions, limitations, and procedure
Ordinance-making power restricted to subjects in Union List and Concurrent List only
Comparison with State Governor's ordinance-making power under Article 213 — similarities and critical differences
Why ordinance power exists: constitutional rationale of legislative urgency during recess

concepts.name: Preconditions for Promulgation: 'Satisfaction' of the President
key_dimensions: The phrase 'if satisfied that circumstances exist' — subjective vs. objective satisfaction debate
Whether 'satisfaction' is justiciable or immune from judicial review (pre vs. post-44th Amendment understanding)
DC Wadhwa case (1987): Supreme Court's ruling that satisfaction must be genuine, not a fraud on the Constitution
Cabinet's role — President acts on aid and advice of Council of Ministers (Article 74); ordinance is effectively Cabinet's decision

concepts.name: Condition of Parliamentary Recess
key_dimensions: Ordinance can only be issued when both Houses (or at least one House) are NOT in session
UPSC trap: 'Both Houses must be in recess' vs. 'at least one House not in session' — Article 123 says Houses are not in session
Distinction between prorogation, adjournment, and dissolution in context of when ordinance power is triggered
Can an ordinance be issued during a Joint Sitting? — edge-case analysis

concepts.name: Legal Status and Force of an Ordinance
key_dimensions: An ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament — it is not subordinate legislation
Ordinance can amend or repeal existing Acts of Parliament during its currency
Ordinance cannot override fundamental rights (subject to same constitutional limitations as ordinary law)
Ordinance cannot amend the Constitution — UPSC frequently tests this limitation

concepts.name: Matters on Which Ordinance CANNOT Be Issued
key_dimensions: Cannot be issued on matters requiring Special Majority (e.g., constitutional amendment under Article 368)
Cannot be issued on matters that require ratification by State Legislatures
Cannot be issued on matters exclusively in State List — critical UPSC trap
Comparison: Governor cannot issue ordinance on matters requiring President's assent for Bills — parallel limitation

concepts.name: Laying Before Parliament: Mandatory Requirement
key_dimensions: Ordinance must be laid before both Houses when Parliament reassembles — Article 123(2)
Consequence of NOT laying the ordinance before Parliament — it does not automatically lapse but becomes a constitutional irregularity
Distinction: 'laying' is mandatory but approval is not automatic — Parliament may disapprove
Order of laying: must be placed before both Houses, not just one

concepts.name: Expiry and Validity Period of an Ordinance
key_dimensions: Ordinance ceases to operate 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles — precise period is critical for MCQs
If both Houses reassemble on different dates, the 6-week period is counted from the LATER date
Ordinance can cease earlier if resolutions of disapproval are passed by both Houses
UPSC trap: Governor's ordinance under Article 213 also ceases after 6 weeks — same period, different authority

concepts.name: Presidential Withdrawal of Ordinance
key_dimensions: President can withdraw an ordinance at any time — Article 123(2)(b)
Withdrawal does not revive any law repealed or amended by the ordinance during its currency — prospective effect only
Whether President can withdraw against Cabinet's advice — theoretically no, given Article 74
Distinction between withdrawal (executive act) and disapproval (legislative act by Parliament)

concepts.name: Re-promulgation of Ordinances: The DC Wadhwa Doctrine
key_dimensions: DC Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): Bihar re-promulgated ordinances repeatedly without placing before legislature — SC called it 'fraud on Constitution'
Re-promulgation to avoid legislative scrutiny violates constitutional scheme of parliamentary democracy
Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017): Seven-judge bench reinforced — re-promulgation is unconstitutional; President/Governor cannot bypass Parliament
UPSC relevance: Re-promulgation is a frequently asked controversy — tests understanding of constitutional morality vs. political practice

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Ordinances
key_dimensions: Ordinances are subject to judicial review — they can be challenged for unconstitutionality (violating fundamental rights, federalism, etc.)
AK Roy v. Union of India (1982): SC held President's satisfaction under Article 123 is NOT immune from judicial review; however, court is reluctant to interfere in genuine urgency cases
Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): Court can examine whether 'satisfaction' was bona fide and whether urgency genuinely existed
Ground of challenge: malafide exercise, lack of legislative competence, violation of Part III

concepts.name: Ordinance vs. Act of Parliament: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: Ordinance is temporary (maximum ~6 months + 6 weeks); Act is permanent unless repealed
Ordinance is unilateral executive action; Act requires bicameral legislative process
Both have equal legal force during ordinance's currency — critical UPSC point
An ordinance can be converted into an Act if Parliament passes it before expiry

concepts.name: Ordinance and Fundamental Rights: Limitations
key_dimensions: Ordinance can be struck down if it violates Part III rights — it has no immunity
However, ordinances related to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)–(6) may be valid
Article 13 definition of 'law' includes ordinances — they are subject to void-for-unconstitutionality rule
Comparison: Presidential Proclamation under Article 352 can suspend Article 19 — ordinance cannot independently do so

concepts.name: Ordinance-Making and Federalism: Concurrent List Complexities
key_dimensions: On Concurrent List subjects, ordinance by President prevails over state law — same as Article 254 rule for central Acts
State cannot pass an ordinance on the same Concurrent subject if Union ordinance occupies the field
President can issue ordinance even on a subject where a State Bill is pending Presidential assent — federal tension
UPSC trap: Compare with Article 356 — President's Rule vs. Ordinance as tools of central intervention

concepts.name: Role of Council of Ministers in Ordinance Promulgation
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment (1978): Made President bound by Cabinet advice even for ordinances — removed discretionary element post-amendment
Ordinance is a Cabinet decision dressed as Presidential act — accountability lies with Cabinet, not President
Can President return the ordinance proposal for reconsideration? — Analogous to Article 111 (return of Bills) — no explicit provision but constitutional convention debated
Ordinance misuse is a political accountability issue, not purely legal — Parliamentary scrutiny is the real check

concepts.name: Disapproval of Ordinance by Parliament
key_dimensions: Both Houses must pass resolutions of disapproval for the ordinance to cease — one House alone cannot kill it
UPSC trap: Unlike a Bill, ordinance disapproval does NOT require Presidential assent — it is a legislative act of rejection
Effect of disapproval is prospective — acts done under the ordinance before disapproval remain valid (unless court strikes down)
Rajya Sabha's role is equal to Lok Sabha in disapproving an ordinance — no special privilege to either House

concepts.name: Ordinance and Constitutional Amendments: The Absolute Bar
key_dimensions: Ordinance CANNOT be used to amend the Constitution — Article 368 requires special legislative procedure
UPSC trap: Ordinance can amend ordinary Acts, but not the Constitution — a frequently confused distinction
Ordinance also cannot bypass provisions requiring ratification by not less than half of State Legislatures (e.g., certain amendments)
This limitation underscores that ordinance power is a 'legislative substitute,' not a 'constituent power'

concepts.name: Ordinance During Dissolution of Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: If Lok Sabha is dissolved, the ordinance can still be issued — as long as Rajya Sabha is also not in session
After dissolution, ordinance must be laid before newly constituted Lok Sabha when it first meets
UPSC trap: Dissolution vs. prorogation — dissolution ends the life of Lok Sabha; ordinance issued during dissolution has longer effective life
Ordinance issued just before dissolution to avoid imminent legislative rejection — constitutional morality question raised in Krishna Kumar Singh

concepts.name: Comparative Analysis: Article 123 vs. Article 213 (Governor's Ordinance Power)
key_dimensions: Governor CANNOT issue ordinance on certain subjects without Presidential instructions — Article 213(1) proviso (e.g., compulsory acquisition, matters affecting High Court)
Governor's ordinance must sometimes be reserved for Presidential consideration — President has oversight over Governor's ordinance but not his own
Both have same 6-week validity after reassembly — same time period is a common MCQ trap
President can direct Governor to withdraw an ordinance — no reverse relationship exists

concepts.name: Ordinance-Making During National Emergency (Article 352)
key_dimensions: During National Emergency, Parliament's legislative power extends to State List — ordinance power correspondingly expands
During President's Rule (Article 356), President exercises State Legislature's power — can issue ordinances for the State as well
UPSC trap: Under Article 356, President legislates for the State by 'Parliament making laws' or by Presidential Ordinance — both routes exist
Emergency does not suspend the ordinance-making procedure — preconditions of Article 123 still apply

concepts.name: Political and Democratic Concerns: Ordinance Raj Debate
key_dimensions: Frequent use of ordinances criticized as 'Ordinance Raj' — bypasses Parliamentary debate and scrutiny
Data-backed analysis: Number of ordinances promulgated vs. converted into Acts — significant proportion lapses without parliamentary approval
Second ARC and Law Commission recommendations: Stricter guidelines for ordinance promulgation; mandatory statement of urgency
UPSC Mains angle: Tension between executive efficiency and legislative supremacy; role of ordinances in parliamentary democracy
